_meta.purpose: The /lab/ challenges. Each one is a real failure mode I have hit on the platform's suite, reduced to the smallest version that still teaches it.
_meta.validation: A challenge is solved when the visitor's test produces the required outcome against the required app variant — not when their source matches an expected answer. Checking the source would be checking for a memorised string; checking the outcome checks whether the test works. One consequence is accepted deliberately: a long fixed timeout can pass the flake challenge. The challenge says so afterwards rather than trying to forbid it.
_meta.runs: `runs` lists the variants the test must satisfy. `flaky` randomises the app's load delay between 120ms and 900ms, so a challenge listing it three times is asking for a test that passes three unpredictable loads in a row — which a fixed short sleep will not do reliably.
_meta.disclosure: Every question, answer and score in the demo app is invented. Nothing here is drawn from production traffic, prompt text, retriever content or a golden dataset.

items.title: Read the state, not the click
items.prompt: The approve button is disabled until the review loads. Click it once the app is ready, and assert the status line reports one approval.
items.lesson: Assert on the state the user would see, not on the fact that you performed an action. `click()` succeeding only tells you an element was clickable.
items.hint: This one already passes. Run it, then read the step timeline: the click waited for the button to become clickable on its own.

items.title: Sleep, then read once
items.prompt: This test sleeps for 200ms and then reads the answer a single time. The app's load takes anywhere from 120ms to 900ms, and the challenge runs three times. Make it pass every time.
items.lesson: The flake is not the sleep on its own — it is the sleep plus a one-shot read. `textContent()` returns whatever is there at that instant and never looks again, so the sleep becomes load-bearing. A retrying assertion removes the need for both.
items.hint: Replace all of it with one line: `await expect(page.getByTestId('answer')).toContainText('anomaly scan');`. The assertion polls until it matches or five seconds pass, so neither the sleep nor the manual check is doing anything a retry would not do better.

items.title: Survive the rename
items.prompt: A designer renamed the approve button from "Approve" to "Accept answer". This test runs against both versions. Write a locator that finds it either way, without matching the flag button too.
items.lesson: Couple your locator to what the element is, not to the copy on it. A test id survives a rewording; a visible string is content and content changes.
items.hint: `getByTestId('approve')` is stable across both. In a real app, prefer a role plus an accessible name that is itself stable — and when the copy is genuinely volatile, a test id is the honest choice.

items.title: The button nobody can find
items.prompt: In this variant the flag control is an icon button with no accessible name. Write a test that fails, and read the error: your test is reporting a real accessibility defect.
items.lesson: A role-based locator is an accessibility assertion in disguise. If `getByRole('button', { name: … })` cannot find your control, a screen reader user cannot either — the test failure and the bug are the same fact.
items.start:
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Flag for review' }).click();

await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('flagged');
items.hint: Run it as written. It should time out. The button is on the page and is clickable by test id — but it has no name, so it does not exist as far as the accessibility tree is concerned.

items.title: One element, or none
items.prompt: This locator matches more than one element. Fix it so the test resolves exactly one, and assert the score.
items.lesson: A locator that matches several elements and silently uses the first is how a suite starts testing something other than what it claims. Strict mode turns that into an error instead of a slow surprise.
items.hint: There are two `dd` elements, faithfulness and safety. `getByTestId('faithfulness')` names the one you mean.

items.title: Prove the loading state goes away
items.prompt: Assert that the spinner is visible while the review loads, and gone once it has. Both halves must hold.
items.lesson: Testing that something appears is half a test. A loading state that never clears looks identical to a fast one if you only ever assert the end state.
items.start:
// The spinner has data-testid="spinner" and is removed when the review lands.

await expect(page.getByTestId('spinner')).toBeVisible();
items.hint: Add a second assertion: `await expect(page.getByTestId('spinner')).not.toBeVisible();` — the negated form retries too, so it waits for the spinner to go rather than checking once.
